title: Do we have a pre-defined threshold at which we would automatically pause an algorithmic program with financial exposure?
description: A board-level oversight question testing whether an organization has a binding, tested kill criterion for an algorithmic program committing its own capital, rather than relying on discretionary judgment after losses have already accumulated.

history.note: Normalized US/UK spelling variants to the American-English house style (schema field names, e.g. organizations_involved, are already American; majority framework citations - NIST, FTC, EEOC, FCRA, BIPA - are American sources).

question_text: Do we have a pre-defined, binding threshold of prediction error or cumulative loss at which an algorithmic program committing our own capital would automatically pause — and has that threshold and pause mechanism ever actually been tested, or does it exist only on paper the way Zillow's apparently did not before its algorithmic home-buying losses reached hundreds of millions of dollars?
rationale: Zillow's algorithmic home-buying program continued scaling through a period of systematic mispricing until losses had already reached hundreds of millions of dollars, resulting in a full business-line shutdown and roughly 2,000 layoffs.
follow_up_actions: Request the current model performance kill-criterion monitoring log for every algorithmic program with direct financial exposure.
Confirm the kill criterion is binding (automatic pause) rather than advisory (a trigger for discussion).
Ask when the kill-criterion mechanism was last actually tested, not just documented.
